# Reference Architecture: Secure Cloud Network Overview (Platform Gainwell)

**← Back to [EAP Home](../../../../README.md) • [Strategy](../../../README.md) • [Guidance](../../README.md) • [Network](./README.md)**

> **TOGAF Artifact Type:** Reference Architecture Document (RAD) — Platform Gainwell Scope
>
> This document provides the overarching reference architecture for the Platform Gainwell Secure Cloud Network. It synthesizes the findings of its child Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs) into an integrated architectural model, establishes the canonical traffic domain diagram, and provides the architecture views that downstream standards, Solution Building Blocks (SBBs), and GRC artifacts reference. It does not define AWS services, security controls, operational configurations, or standards requirements.

### Purpose Statement

This Reference Architecture Document establishes the integrated Secure Cloud Network model for Platform Gainwell — Gainwell Technologies' AWS-based, multi-tenant healthcare technology platform. It synthesizes the structural and behavioral specifications defined in the Secure Cloud Network ABB family into a coherent reference view that serves as:

- The **primary architectural reference** for all Platform Gainwell network security decision-making
- The **parent artifact** that downstream security standards, SBBs, and GRC control mappings reference
- The **canonical source** for the traffic domain model and its visual representation
- The **architectural justification** for the No-DMZ, Zero Trust–aligned network posture

### Business Value

| Value | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Risk reduction** | A structurally defined, explicitly governed network model eliminates the ambiguity that produces ungoverned network paths and undocumented trust assumptions |
| **GRC enablement** | A reference architecture provides the structural foundation that compliance frameworks, audit programs, and risk assessments reference — without requiring security standards to define the architecture themselves |
| **Platform consistency** | All Platform Gainwell workloads, regardless of business unit or application, operate within a common architectural model; consistency is structural, not policy-enforced |
| **Standards readiness** | Security standards for Platform Gainwell are authored against defined architectural elements — domain boundaries, enforcement points, audit emitters — rather than against implicit network concepts |
| **Downstream velocity** | SBB authors, platform engineers, and compliance analysts have a single, authoritative reference model for how the network works architecturally, reducing time spent resolving model ambiguity |

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#scope-and-applicability]

### Scope and Applicability

This reference architecture governs the network security architecture of **Platform Gainwell** — Gainwell's AWS-hosted, multi-account, multi-tenant platform. It applies to all workloads hosted on Platform Gainwell, all accounts within the Platform Gainwell AWS Organization, and all traffic flows that cross a Platform Gainwell network boundary.

It does not govern:

- Enterprise network architecture outside Platform Gainwell's AWS Organization
- On-premises or hybrid network architecture
- Workloads hosted outside the Platform Gainwell platform, even if operated by Gainwell

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#vision-statement]

### Vision Statement

Platform Gainwell's network architecture establishes a fully explicit, continuously verified traffic governance model in which no inter-system communication is permitted by default, every flow traverses an appropriate domain boundary before reaching its destination, and no implicit trust is granted based on network location.

The target state is a network architecture where:

- Every traffic flow is classified, governed, and auditable by domain
- No workload is directly reachable from outside without traversing an application-layer boundary
- No cross-boundary communication exists outside a defined domain governance model
- The network architecture expresses the organization's security intent without relying on perimeter-as-protection assumptions
page_texts.10:
[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#strategic-objectives]

### Strategic Objectives

| Objective | Architectural Expression |
|-----------|-------------------------|
| **Eliminate implicit trust** | No domain boundary grants access based on network position alone; verified identity and explicit policy are required at every boundary |
| **Classify all traffic** | Every flow on Platform Gainwell is classified into one of four explicitly governed domains; unclassified traffic has no permit path |
| **Eliminate the DMZ** | No semi-trusted network zone exists; external traffic terminates at an application-layer boundary, not at a firewall handoff to a less-protected zone |
| **Make security intent structural** | Network security properties are expressed as architectural elements — domain boundaries, enforcement points, audit emitters — not as configuration policies that can drift |
| **Enable governance observability** | Every domain boundary produces observable events; the network architecture is observable by design, not instrumented retrospectively |
page_texts.11:
[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#governing-architecture-decisions]

### Governing Architecture Decisions

This reference architecture realizes the five architectural invariants established in **ADR-SEC-PG-001** (Secure Cloud Network Architecture for Platform Gainwell):

| Invariant | Expression in This Architecture |
|-----------|--------------------------------|
| No traditional DMZ | External traffic terminates at Domain 1 (External-In); no semi-trusted intermediate zone exists |
| Application-layer controls authoritative for ingress | All ingress access decisions are made at the application layer, not the network layer |
| All traffic explicitly classified | The four-domain model provides an exhaustive classification for all Platform Gainwell traffic |
| Implicit trust prohibited at all boundaries | Every domain boundary requires explicit policy and verified identity; network position alone confers no access |
| Cross-domain traffic requires explicit policy artifact | Every authorized domain traversal is governed by a named, registered policy artifact |
page_texts.12:
[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#architectural-principles]

### Architectural Principles

These principles govern all Platform Gainwell network architecture decisions and design choices:

| Principle | Application to Network Architecture |
|-----------|-------------------------------------|
| **Zero Trust** (NIST SP 800-207) | All four traffic domains enforce per-flow or per-request verification; no persistent trust is established by network topology |
| **Fail Closed by Default** | Domain boundaries fail to a deny posture; no boundary fails open |
| **Explicit Authentication and Authorization** | Every boundary cross requires identity verification and policy evaluation; network adjacency is not authorization |
| **Separation of Control and Data Planes** | Decision-making is separable from enforcement; audit emission is separate from both |
| **Least Privilege by Default** | Absence of a permit policy results in a deny; no default-allow path exists for any traffic class |
| **Defense in Depth** | Network-layer controls provide defense-in-depth support for application-layer domain boundaries; neither is the sole control for a given flow |
| **Assume Breach** | Architecture is designed to limit lateral movement and blast radius; cross-domain authorization is independent at each domain |

### Business Context

Gainwell Technologies delivers healthcare technology solutions to state Medicaid agencies, managed care organizations, and federal health programs. Platform Gainwell is the AWS-based platform that hosts these workloads. The nature of this business establishes the following architectural context:

- **Regulatory environment:** Workloads on Platform Gainwell routinely process Protected Health Information (PHI) and Personally Identifiable Information (PII) under HIPAA and state equivalents, CMS program data under ARC-AMPE v1.02 (successor to MARS-E 2.0), and Federal Tax Information (FTI) under IRS Publication 1075 for applicable programs
- **Multi-tenancy:** Platform Gainwell hosts workloads for multiple Gainwell business units and programs within a shared infrastructure model; the network architecture must provide tenant isolation without requiring separate physical infrastructure
- **External connectivity:** Platform Gainwell workloads exchange data with state agency partner systems, CMS federal systems, managed care organizations, and Gainwell's own services outside its AWS Organization; all such connectivity is classified as External-In or Internal-Out domain traffic

| AWS multi-account organization | Account boundaries are the primary unit of isolation; the network architecture uses AWS account structure to establish trust zone boundaries |
| Multi-tenant workload model | Workloads from different tenants may co-locate in the same VPC or account; the architecture must govern inter-tenant traffic even within shared infrastructure |
| Cloud-native, no on-premises dependency | No hybrid network extension is required; the trust boundary is the AWS Organization boundary |
| Identity-centric security model | AWS identity primitives (IAM roles, service accounts, OIDC-federated identities) provide the workload identity foundation the domain authorization model requires |

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#41-architectural-foundation]

### 4.1 Architectural Foundation

Platform Gainwell's network architecture is founded on two premises that together distinguish it from a conventional enterprise network security model:

**Premise 1: No-DMZ**

Traditional enterprise network security separates external traffic from internal traffic through a DMZ — a network zone of intermediate trust positioned between the external perimeter firewall and the internal network. The DMZ model relies on network location as a security property: workloads in the DMZ are considered less trusted than internal workloads, and the transition between zones enforces a degree of control.

Platform Gainwell does not operate a DMZ. External traffic terminates at the application-layer Domain 1 (External-In) boundary, where authentication and authorization are performed. There is no network zone between the external perimeter and the authorized backend workload; access is granted or denied by the application layer, not by placement in an intermediate zone.

The rationale is architectural: a DMZ grants ambient trust to traffic that has passed a network-layer perimeter check. Platform Gainwell's Zero Trust posture requires that trust be verified at the application layer regardless of prior network-layer checks. A DMZ intermediate zone would create a class of traffic with greater-than-zero implicit trust, which violates ADR-SEC-PG-001's implicit-trust prohibition.

**Premise 2: Four-Domain Traffic Governance**

Every traffic flow on Platform Gainwell belongs to exactly one of four explicitly governed domains. This classification is exhaustive — any traffic that cannot be classified into one of the four domains is non-conforming and has no permit path. The four-domain model ensures that no traffic class exists outside architectural governance, eliminating the "ungoverned middle ground" that exists in many enterprise network models between defined security zones.

The four domains, their authoritative definitions, and their governing ABBs are established in *§4.3* and realized in the Structural Network ABB ([GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-ABB](./GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-ABB-v1.md)) and the Traffic Control Domains ABB ([GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-TRAFFIC-CONTROL-ABB](./GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-TRAFFIC-CONTROL-ABB-v1.md)).

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#42-structural-network-model]

### 4.2 Structural Network Model

The Platform Gainwell structural network model organizes the AWS environment into three logical layers, defined by the Secure Cloud Network ABB ([GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-ABB](./GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-ABB-v1.md)):

| Layer | Element | Role in Network Architecture |
|-------|---------|------------------------------|
| **Organization Layer** | AWS Organization | Defines the Platform Gainwell trust boundary; traffic crossing this boundary is External-In or Internal-Out by definition |
| **Account Layer** | AWS Accounts | Tenant and capability isolation units; traffic crossing an account boundary within the Organization traverses Domain 3 (East-West) |
| **VPC Layer** | VPCs within accounts | Workload deployment environments; traffic between workloads within the same VPC is Domain 4 (Intra-VPC) |

**Classification of traffic by structural boundary:**

| Traffic Crosses | Domain | Domain Name |
|----------------|--------|-------------|
| AWS Organization boundary (inbound) | Domain 1 | External-In |
| AWS Organization boundary (outbound) | Domain 2 | Internal-Out |
| AWS Account or VPC boundary (within Organization) | Domain 3 | East-West |
| No VPC boundary (within same VPC) | Domain 4 | Intra-VPC |

> **Same-account multi-VPC note:** The classification above reflects the common case. Where multiple VPCs exist within the same AWS account for distinct logical applications, domain classification follows the VPC boundary definition established in the Structural Network ABB rather than the account boundary alone. Edge-case topologies (AWS RAM shared subnets, cross-account VPC sharing constructs) are resolved during architectural review against the Structural Network ABB.

Network-layer structural details — VPC topology, account organization, transit hub placement, and IP addressing model — are specified in the Secure Cloud Network ABB. This reference architecture treats those details as realized infrastructure and describes how they support the domain governance model.

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#43-traffic-control-domain-model]

### 4.3 Traffic Control Domain Model

The four traffic control domains are the primary security governance elements of Platform Gainwell's network architecture. Each domain is governed by an independently evaluated authorization policy; no domain inherits authorization from a domain the traffic has already traversed. The domain model is specified in the Traffic Control Domains ABB ([GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-TRAFFIC-CONTROL-ABB](./GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-TRAFFIC-CONTROL-ABB-v1.md)).

**Domain 1 — External-In (Ingress)**

Governs traffic originating outside the Platform Gainwell organizational trust boundary and destined for a hosted workload or service. The application layer is solely authoritative for access decisions in this domain — network-layer constructs (routing rules, security group permits, IP allowlisting) establish connectivity prerequisites but do not constitute access authorization. All external traffic terminates at the Domain 1 boundary before any inward routing occurs; the domain model defines no path from an external origin to a backend workload that bypasses this boundary.

**Domain 2 — Internal-Out (Egress)**

Governs traffic originating from a Platform Gainwell workload and destined for an endpoint outside the organizational trust boundary. Egress authorization is governed by a registered egress policy that authorizes specific workload identities to communicate with specific external destination classes. The domain model defines outbound flows through registered policy; it does not define an authorization path for workloads whose egress destinations have not been registered.

**Domain 3 — East-West (Inter-VPC / Inter-Account)**

Governs traffic between workloads, services, or accounts wholly within the Platform Gainwell organizational trust boundary but crossing a VPC or account boundary. East-West authorization is governed by service identity policy — VPC membership and AWS account affiliation establish routing scope but do not constitute authorization. All East-West flows are mediated through a centralized enforcement point; the domain model defines no direct VPC-to-VPC or account-to-account authorization path that bypasses this mediation.

**Domain 4 — Intra-VPC (Workload-to-Workload)**

Governs traffic between workloads co-located within the same VPC. VPC co-location is a routing condition, not an authorization condition; the domain model does not define shared VPC membership as a grant of lateral communication rights. Domain 4 is the innermost domain — traffic from external origins or cross-boundary service calls enters Domain 4 after traversing the applicable outer domain boundary.

The following C4-level diagram depicts the Platform Gainwell Secure Cloud Network traffic domain model. Colors indicate domain affiliation: **orange** = Domain 1 (External-In), **blue** = Domain 2 (Internal-Out), **green** = Domain 3 (East-West), **yellow** = Domain 4 (Intra-VPC).

> **Architectural scope:** This diagram depicts domain boundary positions and traffic flow classification. It does not specify AWS services, routing configurations, or enforcement tooling. Account A and Account B are illustrative of the multi-account model; actual account topology is defined in the Structural Network ABB.

**Common traffic flow paths depicted:**

| Path | Domains Traversed | Description |
|------|-------------------|-------------|
| External user → Workload A (same account) | Domain 1 only | Standard single-account ingress; authorized by Domain 1 boundary |

| Workload A → External destination | Domain 4 → Domain 2 | Outbound call; governed by registered egress policy in Domain 2 |

## 5. Architecture Views

The following views describe the Platform Gainwell Secure Cloud Network architecture from four complementary perspectives. Each view addresses different stakeholder concerns without duplicating the structural or behavioral specifications contained in the child ABBs.
page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#51-network-architecture-view]

### 5.1 Network Architecture View

**Concern addressed:** How is the platform's network environment structured, and how do structural elements (accounts, VPCs, boundaries) relate to the domain model?

**Key architectural elements:**

| Element | Structural Role | Domain Relationship |
|---------|----------------|---------------------|
| **AWS Organization** | Defines the outermost trust container; its boundary is the organizational trust perimeter | Crossing this boundary inbound = Domain 1; outbound = Domain 2 |
| **AWS Accounts** | Tenant and capability isolation units within the Organization | Crossing an account boundary internally = Domain 3 |
| **Platform Networking Account** | Centralized account hosting transit routing and East-West enforcement infrastructure | Houses the Domain 3 Enforcement Point |
| **Workload Accounts** | Accounts hosting Platform Gainwell applications and services | Domain 4 governs intra-VPC traffic within each workload account |
| **VPCs** | Workload deployment environments within accounts | VPC boundaries define Domain 3 entry for cross-VPC calls; workloads within a VPC are in Domain 4 |
| **Ingress Edge** | The organizational ingress point at which Domain 1 enforcement is positioned | All external traffic terminates here; no external routing reaches a workload account directly |
| **Egress Edge** | The organizational egress point at which Domain 2 enforcement is positioned | All outbound workload traffic routes through here; no workload account has a direct external path |

**This view does not define:** VPC CIDR ranges, subnet topology, specific AWS networking services, or routing table configurations. Those details are addressed in the Structural Network ABB and downstream SBBs.

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#52-security-control-boundary-view]

### 5.2 Security Control Boundary View

**Concern addressed:** Where are the security control boundaries in the network architecture, what does each boundary do, and how do they compose into a defense-in-depth model?

The Platform Gainwell control boundary model is built from the **Control Boundary Pattern (CBP)** defined in the Traffic Control Domains ABB. Every domain boundary exhibits four structural components: a Decision Engine, an Enforcement Point, an Audit Emitter, and an Exception Handler. The model below describes how those components combine across the four-domain architecture:

```
External Origin
     │
     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Domain 1 Control Boundary — External-In                         │
│  Decision Engine: Application-layer authN/authZ                  │
│  Enforcement Point: Organizational ingress edge                  │
│  Audit Emitter: Every access decision (permit + deny)            │
│  Exception Handler: Fail to deny on Decision Engine unavailable  │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ Policy Assertion
                             ▼
           ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
           │  Domain 4 Control Boundary          │
           │  (Same-account Workload Target)      │
           │  Decision Engine: Segmentation policy│
           │  Enforcement Point: Workload-level   │
           └────────────────────────────────────┘

OR (cross-account path):

                             │ Policy Assertion
                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Domain 3 Control Boundary — East-West                           │
│  Decision Engine: Service identity policy                        │
│  Enforcement Point: Centralized transit (no direct peering)      │
│  Audit Emitter: Every cross-boundary authorization               │
│  Exception Handler: Fail to deny on Decision Engine unavailable  │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ Policy Assertion
                             ▼
           ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
           │  Domain 4 Control Boundary          │
           │  (Cross-account Workload Target)     │
           └────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Key properties of the composed control boundary model:**

- **Defense in depth:** Network-layer controls (firewalling, routing constraints) provide a supporting layer; the application-layer domain boundary provides the authoritative control. Neither layer alone constitutes the full security property.
- **Domain sovereignty:** Each boundary makes an independent authorization decision; a permit at an outer boundary does not carry authority into an inner boundary.
- **Uniform failure posture:** All four boundaries fail to a deny posture; no boundary in any domain fails open.
- **End-to-end auditability:** Each boundary in a flow's path emits audit records; the Policy Assertion's correlation identifier links those records across domain boundaries.

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#53-trust-and-identity-view]

### 5.3 Trust and Identity View

**Concern addressed:** What identity model underpins the platform's domain authorization decisions, and how does trust propagate (or not propagate) across domain boundaries?

**Trust boundary definition:** The Platform Gainwell trust boundary is the AWS Organization boundary. Traffic originating from within the Organization boundary is assigned a Platform Gainwell workload identity by the platform's authoritative identity fabric. Traffic originating outside the Organization boundary carries no inherent trust; its identity is verified at the Domain 1 boundary.

**Identity categories and domain roles:**

| Identity Category | Domain Role |
|-------------------|-------------|
| **Human user identity** (federated, via IAM Identity Center or equivalent) | Authorization subject for Domain 1 (External-In) for user-originating ingress |
| **Workload identity** (IAM role or service account issued to a specific workload) | Authorization subject for Domains 2 (egress policy), 3 (East-West service policy), and 4 (segmentation policy) |
| **Partner / external system identity** (verified by the Domain 1 Decision Engine; may be federated or mutual-TLS client-authenticated) | Authorization subject for Domain 1; does not carry into inner domains without re-verification |
| **Service-to-service identity** (workload identity asserted by the calling workload) | Authorization subject for Domain 3 East-West policy; the architectural model defines workload identity issued by the platform's authoritative identity fabric as the authorization subject — IP-derived or self-asserted identity is not the defined basis for East-West authorization in this domain model |

**Trust propagation model:**

Trust does not automatically propagate between domains. When traffic transitions from one domain to another, the receiving domain's Decision Engine makes an independent authorization determination using the identity context propagated via the **Policy Assertion** from the outgoing domain. The Policy Assertion (defined in the Traffic Control Domains ABB §5.4) carries the verified identity context; it does not carry the authorization decision from the prior domain.

**What this means structurally:**

- A user identity verified at Domain 1 is propagated in the Policy Assertion to Domain 4 — but Domain 4's segmentation policy determines whether that identity may communicate with co-located workloads; Domain 1's permit decision does not establish this.
- A workload in Domain 4 initiating an East-West call asserts its workload identity at the Domain 3 boundary; Domain 3's Decision Engine evaluates that identity against cross-boundary service policy independently.

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#54-observability-view]

### 5.4 Observability View

**Concern addressed:** What observable signals does the network architecture produce, and where in the architecture are those signals generated?

The observability model is defined by the Traffic Control Domains ABB (§8). This view describes *where in the architecture* those signals originate and their relationship to the security operations infrastructure.

**Signal generation points:**

| Domain Boundary | Primary Observable Signal Classes | Architectural Significance |
|----------------|----------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Domain 1 — External-In** | Every inbound access decision (permit + deny), Authentication events, Exception Handler events | Provides the primary visibility surface for external threat actors, unauthorized access attempts, and API abuse |
| **Domain 2 — Internal-Out** | Every egress authorization event (permit + deny), Data volume context, Exception Handler events | Primary detection surface for data exfiltration; every external data movement is observable by workload identity |
| **Domain 3 — East-West** | Every cross-boundary service authorization event, Source and target service identities, Exception Handler events | Detection surface for lateral movement; all authorized cross-account service communications are individually recorded |
| **Domain 4 — Intra-VPC** | Policy-significant segmentation events (proportional to sensitivity classification), Exception Handler events | Innermost detection surface; sensitivity-proportionate to reduce operational noise while maintaining PHI/PII visibility |
| **Domain Handoff Points** | Policy Assertion transit events with audit correlation identifiers | Enables end-to-end request reconstruction across domain boundaries without requiring correlation by content |

**Audit path structural property (defined in GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-TRAFFIC-CONTROL-ABB §5.2):**

The Control Boundary Pattern defines the Audit Emitter's output path as architecturally separate from the governed data plane workload. This structural property is what enables the SecOps collection infrastructure to receive domain boundary signals regardless of workload state — a workload's operational condition does not gate the production or delivery of its boundary audit records.

**What this view does not define:** Collection mechanisms, SIEM platforms, alert logic, detection rules, or operational response procedures. Those are addressed by the SecOps Reference Architecture ([GUID-SEC-SECOPS-GEN-ARCH-REF-1.1.01](../SecOps/GUID-SEC-SECOPS-GEN-ARCH-REF-1.1.01.md)) and downstream operational standards.

## 7. Realization Approach

This section describes the architectural sequencing for realizing Platform Gainwell's Secure Cloud Network — not an implementation plan. The sequence is governed by dependency: later phases depend on capabilities established in earlier phases.

> **Scope boundary:** Specific AWS services, configurations, tooling, and operational procedures are addressed in the relevant SBBs and platform engineering documentation. This section describes what must exist architecturally before what, not how it is built.

**Phase 1 — Foundation (Structural Network Model)**

The structural network model (account organization, VPC topology, organizational trust boundary) must be established before any domain governance can be enforced. Domain boundaries can only be positioned when the network structure they govern exists. The Structural Network ABB ([GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-ABB](./GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-ABB-v1.md)) governs this phase's architectural requirements.

**Phase 2 — Organizational Boundary Governance (Domains 1 and 2)**

With the structural model in place, the External-In (Domain 1) and Internal-Out (Domain 2) boundaries govern traffic at the organizational perimeter. These are the highest-priority domain boundaries because they govern the most sensitive traffic class (external ingress and outbound data movement). The API Gateway ABB ([GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04](./GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04.md)) and planned Egress Governance ABB/SBB address Domain 1 and Domain 2 realization respectively.

**Phase 3 — Cross-Boundary Governance (Domain 3)**

East-West governance establishes mediated routing for all cross-VPC and cross-account traffic. This phase depends on Phase 1 establishing the account boundaries and Phase 2 establishing that organizational boundary traffic is governed; it introduces governance for the inter-account traffic class. The Microsegmentation Guidance ([GUID-SEC-NETWORK-MICROSEG-2.2.03](./GUID-SEC-NETWORK-MICROSEG-2.2.03.md)) addresses aspects of East-West realization.

**Phase 4 — Workload-Level Governance (Domain 4)**

Intra-VPC segmentation governance is the final phase because it depends on the outer domain boundaries being in place — Domain 4 is the innermost domain and is reached only after applicable outer boundaries have been traversed. The Microsegmentation Guidance and planned Intra-VPC SBB address Domain 4 realization.

**Phase 5 — Observable Architecture**

End-to-end observability across all four domain boundaries, including cross-domain audit correlation, represents the architectural completeness state. This phase depends on all four domain boundaries being established (Phases 1–4) and the SecOps collection infrastructure being deployed to receive domain boundary signals.

## 8. Governance and Compliance Alignment

> This section identifies how Platform Gainwell's network architecture supports compliance obligations. It does not constitute a compliance assessment, gap analysis, or control mapping — those are GRC artifacts that reference this architecture as their foundation.

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-PG-CLOUD-NETWORK-OVERARCHING-RAD.V1.md#compliance-framework-alignment]

### Compliance Framework Alignment

| Framework | Obligation | How This Architecture Addresses It |
|-----------|------------|-------------------------------------|
| **HIPAA §164.312(e)(1)** | Transmission Security | Every domain boundary establishes encryption in transit as an architectural property for PHI-bearing flows; the fail-closed posture ensures that boundary degradation does not produce an unencrypted bypass path |
| **HIPAA §164.312(b)** | Audit Controls | The Audit Emitter is a required structural component of every domain boundary; §5.4 (Observability View) establishes the audit signal model that downstream HIPAA audit controls reference |
| **HIPAA §164.308(a)(4)** | Information Access Management | Every domain boundary requires authenticated identity and explicit policy authorization before access is granted; the Policy Assertion model provides the structural representation of access authorization |
| **HIPAA §164.312(a)(1)** | Access Control | Domain-sovereign authorization at every boundary; no implicit access from network position; workload segmentation policy in Domain 4 enforces least-privilege access between co-located workloads |
| **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — SC-7** | Boundary Protection | All four domain boundaries establish monitored, policy-enforced access points at organizational perimeter and internal network boundaries; fail-closed behavior addresses SC-7's requirement for boundary protection when controls are unavailable |
| **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — AC-4** | Information Flow Enforcement | Domain-specific Control Authority Models govern information flow at every boundary; the network architecture enforces information flow policy at the structural level |
| **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — SC-8** | Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity | Domain boundary encryption requirements address this control for all four domains, with PHI/PII-bearing paths receiving explicit attention in the External-In and East-West domain specifications |
| **NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — AU-2/AU-9/AU-12** | Audit Events / Protection / Generation | Audit Emitter structural component addresses AU-2 (what to audit) and AU-12 (generation); architecturally separate output path addresses AU-9 (audit protection) |
| **NIST SP 800-207** | Zero Trust Architecture | Domain sovereignty (no inherited authorization), per-flow verification (Decision Engine structure), Policy Assertion model (explicit verification artifact), and fail-closed posture (assume-breach operationalization) all instantiate NIST SP 800-207 §2.1–2.3 |
| **ARC-AMPE v1.02** | CMS Transmission Security and Access Control for PHI | Domain 1 (External-In) constraints, the Policy Assertion model, and the Domain 2 (Internal-Out) egress policy model address ARC-AMPE access control and audit obligations for ACA, Medicaid, and Partner Entity data flowing through Platform Gainwell |

## 10. Assumptions and Dependencies

| ID | Assumption / Dependency | Implication If Not Met |
|----|------------------------|------------------------|
| ASM-RAD-01 | The Platform Gainwell AWS Organization boundary is the authoritative trust boundary; no AWS account within the Organization is considered an external source | If Organization boundary is not the trust boundary (e.g., if individual accounts have external trust grants), Domain 1 must be repositioned and the structural model revised |
| ASM-RAD-02 | The platform's workload identity fabric issues verifiable, non-IP-derived identities to workloads at deployment time | Without workload identity, Domain 3 (East-West) and Domain 4 (Intra-VPC) authorization for PHI/PII-bearing flows cannot be performed at the structural level; IP-layer controls become the only available mechanism |
| ASM-RAD-03 | Centralized transit routing infrastructure for East-West traffic exists as a platform capability; no workload account can route directly to another workload account outside this infrastructure | Without centralized routing, Domain 3 enforcement cannot be architecturally positioned; cross-account traffic would have no defined governance point |
| ASM-RAD-04 | The SecOps Reference Architecture provides a telemetry collection infrastructure that accepts domain boundary audit signals from all four domains | Without this infrastructure, the observability view (§5.4) cannot be realized; domain boundaries would produce audit signals with no guaranteed collection path |
| ASM-RAD-05 | Workloads are onboarded through a platform process that registers their traffic profiles (ingress contract, egress destinations, inter-service dependencies) before production admission | Without pre-registration, Decision Engines have no policy to evaluate against; unregistered workloads cannot be governed by any domain boundary |
| ASM-RAD-06 | A platform exception management process exists for workloads that cannot immediately conform to all domain governance properties | Without an exception pathway, legacy or transitional workloads produce invisible non-conformance rather than governed exceptions |
